data.hypothesis: The prior correct candidate used 256 threads processing 2048 inputs per CTA and added a scratch-backed stage when it produced more than 1024 partials; it measured 10.216 µs over three samples versus the baseline's 47.079 µs. This candidate doubles first-pass work to 4096 inputs per CTA while keeping 256 threads. At n=4,194,304 that yields 1024 partials, which one final 256-thread CTA can sum, testing whether avoiding the extra stage and launch outweighs increased per-CTA work and a single-CTA final pass.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use the prior candidate as a measured comparison, not as proof that its particular tile or hierarchy caused the observed timing.
memory_lessons.claim: The prior candidate was correct across 10 required cases and had a three-sample mean of 10.216 µs; the baseline was also correct and measured 47.079 µs. The next distinct comparison can test larger first-pass work and a two-stage large-input hierarchy.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Compare the 4096-input CTA tile and one-block final sum against the prior 2048-input tile with its conditional extra stage.

data.notes: This candidate changes only src/candidate.cu. It writes at most ceil(n/4096) scratch partials, handles first-pass tails with bounds checks, and directly writes the output when the first pass has one block. No candidate correctness or timing result is available before controller validation.
transformations: Replace the repeated 128-element baseline passes with a coalesced 256-thread first pass in which each CTA covers 4096 inputs using tail-safe loads.
For multiple first-pass blocks, sum their scratch-backed partials with one non-atomic 256-thread final kernel; write directly to output when the first pass has one block.
Retain the device-to-device copy for n<=1 and use only the first scratch region, bounded by the number of first-pass blocks.
